instructions: For each question below: (1) FULL ABLATION — using only the stem and options, with no access to the source pack, decide whether the answer can be determined. If it can, the question fails. (2) BLIND RE-ANSWER — read the pack, then choose an option without seeing the answer key. Disagreement with the key, or a defensible case for a second option, rejects the item.

questions.stem: Two external walls are built from the same two layers in the same thicknesses, but one is twice the area of the other. According to the text, how do they stand against the guidance?

options.text: The smaller wall is the more likely to be adequate, since less heat crosses it.
The larger wall is the more likely to be adequate, since its heat flow is spread over more area.
They stand identically, because the quantity the guidance limits does not depend on the wall’s area.
Neither can be judged until the temperature difference on the day is known.

blocks.text: Heat flow through layered building walls

When the two sides of a wall are held at different temperatures, heat flows steadily from the warmer side to the cooler one. In the steady state the rate of flow no longer changes with time, and the same quantity of heat passes through every layer of the wall each second. The flow is driven by the temperature difference across the wall and is opposed by the wall's thermal resistance.

Figure 1. A single-layer wall. Heat passes from the warm side to the cool side at a steady rate.   Single layer thickness d, conductivity lambda Warm side higher temperature Cool side lower temperature

R = d / lambda;   Q = A * dT / R_total Thermal resistance of one layer, and the resulting rate of heat flow through the wall. R thermal resistance of a layer per unit area, in square metre kelvin per watt d thickness of the layer in metres lambda conductivity of the layer's material in watts per metre kelvin A wall area in square metres dT temperature difference between the two sides in kelvin Q rate of heat flow in watts

A wall built from several layers behaves like a chain: the same heat passes through each layer in turn, and the resistances of the layers are added together to give the total resistance of the wall. Because the resistances are added, the order in which the layers are arranged does not change the total. A layer of low conductivity contributes a large resistance even when it is thin, while a thick layer of high conductivity may contribute very little.

Figure 2. A two-layer wall of area 18 square metres, with the warm side held 20 kelvin above the cool side.   Brick layer thickness 0.24 m, conductivity 0.60 watts per metre kelvin Insulation layer thickness 0.08 m, conductivity 0.05 watts per metre kelvin Wall area 18 square metres Temperature difference 20 kelvin

Because the total resistance is a sum of positive terms, it is always larger than the resistance of any single layer taken alone. Adding a further layer can therefore only reduce the rate of heat flow, never increase it. Doubling the thickness of one layer doubles that layer's resistance, but it does not double the total resistance of the wall, because the other layers are unchanged.

Performance is usually quoted not as a resistance but as a U-value: the rate at which heat crosses one square metre of the wall for each kelvin of temperature difference, which is one divided by the total thermal resistance. Because it is stated per square metre and per kelvin, a wall’s U-value does not depend on how large the wall is or on how cold the day is. The guidance this text follows treats an external wall as adequate when its U-value does not exceed 0.28 watts per square metre kelvin.
